A party that wants the summit instead scrambles up and right from the tree belay onto the ridge and follows Windsor Ridge
name: Wonderous Wanderer
overview: Reaches the crest of Windsor Ridge in four pitches. P1 (5.0, 35 m) is easy ledgy ground. P2 (5.10b, 35 m) traverses left about 5 m, then follows a crack. P3 (5.10a, 38 m) goes up a gully to a fine splitter hand crack. P4 (5.6, 15 m) heads up and left to a tree belay. Scramble up and right to the rid

approach: Take the trail from Moraine Lake to Sentinel Pass. Grand Sentinel stands beyond the pass toward Paradise Valley and is visible to the south from the trail. descent: After topping out the headwall, join the Lady Macdonald scramble on the summit ridge. Follow the hikers' scramble trail down to the entrance of Cougar Creek, where the route began.

overview: Ridge route on Lady Macdonald. Hike from the trailhead to a first 8 m step, easy 5th class, then keep on the path across stone, loose scree and soil until a big cliff rises above. Ford the river and look for the yellow sign marking the trail, then follow a narrow trail on the south side of the valley for two hours or so, then turn west up a scree gully and cross Woolley Shoulder.
descent: Descend by the Japanese Route. From the summit, follow the ridge south through a notch and a couple of short rappels to a deeper notch and the main rappel gully, then make a long series of rappels down it to the yellow rock ledge. name: Northeast Ridge
overview: Best-rock line to the summit, though loose rock still must be dodged, especially while descending. Plan a full day; finding the way down after nightfall is unrealistic with no GPS track on hand. An edging arete starts at a pinned anchor; test every hold, as gear is absent until another fixed anchor

approach: From the parking lot, take the Cavell Meadows trail and then head up the moraines to the foot of the east ridge. The scramble to the base is loose and unpleasant, especially in the dark. A snow couloir flanks the ridge on one side and the north face on the other.
descent: Most parties reverse the route by downclimbing. The alternative is to continue over the summit and down the west ridge, a much larger traverse that stays on the ridge until the col with Mount Sorrow, because dropping off sooner can lead into cliff bands, and which ends in the Tonquin Valley.
name: East Ridge
overview: A well-known Canadian Rockies ridge climb that follows the left skyline of the mountain. Graded 5.3 with moderate snow.

From the summit, the way down is a rappel descent on the north side of the peak, starting at a bolted anchor above a gentle gully. Rappel the gully on bolted anchors until it steepens, then walk up the short, easy ramp

overview: Conrad Kain climbed Mount Louis by this line in 1916. The start is under the rightmost of three low scoops; trend upward and leftward via the centre one. approach: Hike through Paradise Valley to Lake Annette, pass around the lake's right-hand shore and angle up to the toe of the buttress that separates the north face from the Sphinx face. A short cliff band guards the face; find a gap in it and climb one brief pitch at low fifth class to reach easier ground.
descent: From the top of the buttress, slog loose scree on the glacier's left side to the crest of the ridge, where the East Ridge route arrives above the Black Towers. Continue along the corniced summit ridge to the top, then descend the easy southwest slopes to Moraine Lake. A long walk along the Moraine L
name: Greenwood-Jones
overview: Rock climbing on Mount Temple, up the buttress that separates the Sphinx face from the north face. Stone quality varies, escape from high on the line is hard, and slow parties risk a bivy. Pitches are mainly fifth class, easier low down and a bit harder higher, until a level ledge system roughly 3/4

approach: From the Paradise Valley trailhead, hike up the valley and around Lake Annette, past the starts of Greenwood-Jones and the Sphinx face. Continue up steep scree nearly to the notch beneath the Aemmer Couloir, then trend uphill on dirty ledges into an obvious gully that rises to the right. Scramble th
descent: The buttress leads to the upper East Ridge, below the Black Towers, and the route continues up the towers to the summit ice cap and the summit. Descend the southwest ridge to Sentinel Pass, drop north into Paradise Valley and follow the trail signs back to the trailhead.
name: Squashed Bones
overview: Mt. Temple's northeast buttress, the gentlest line on its North Face. Six to ten roped pitches, linked by scrambling, reach the point where the buttress turns south to meet the upper third of the East Ridge. Choose the cleanest rock at 5.8 or easier. approach: The route starts at the col between Mount Whyte and Devil's Thumb, reached above Lake Agnes. From the col, scramble up talus on climber's left into a small basin that gives access to the east ridge, then follow the ridge.
descent: A short steep wall just below the summit is the hardest step. Descend the north ridge to the col between Whyte and Mount Niblock, then pick a way down through the cliff bands back to Lake Agnes.
name: Perren Route (East Ridge)
overview: A relatively easy day mostly of scrambling along the ridge, with moderate climbing only close to the summit. Route-finding is interesting and the rock is loose in places. A brief, steep wall just below the summit goes at 5.6 and can be wet. Descend the north ridge to the col between Whyte and Nibloc

approach: From the Moraine Lake parking area, follow the Consolation Lakes trail to the north shore of the southern Consolation Lake, then ascend the giant scree slope to the foot of the wall. The line starts left of a big gully and works up corners and faces to the summit of a large detached pillar beneath t
descent: Go down the north ridge from the summit, all the way to the Tower of Babel's descent gully. Expect it to be slow and involves some downclimbing, rappels off single-bolt anchors and plenty of scree.
name: East Face
overview: A huge face with no detailed description available, climbed by many as a Rockies rite of passage. Place belays carefully, avoid the route if snow lies on the ledges, and note that a large ledge cuts across the whole face and offers an escape prior to the serious difficulties. One pitch is muddy. descent: From the summit, descend the southeast ridge to a rappel anchor on a slung block, then continue down the ridge, bypassing difficulties mostly on the right. At the col between Colin and the next peak to the south, follow cairned scree down to a creek bed and follow it down to the hut.
name: NW Traverse
overview: From the Hawk col, scramble third and fourth class ground to a pedestal, beyond which the ridge is knife-edged. Follow it directly, pulling around it, at an easy fifth-class standard, until an anchor appears. Mostly third class with easy fourth and fifth class steps, moved together on a short rope o

descent: Three descents are possible. One traverses behind Tuzo and Allen and goes down the Schiesser Route to Moraine Lake. Another follows the glacier on the back side, weaves down the cliff bands to the lake below and leaves by the Tokumn Creek trail, which is long and not maintained throughout. The third
name: Flying Buttress

approach: Leave the Wates-Gibson hut on the clear trail heading south to the moraine. Climb the moraine's steep nose on its trail until the path dies out, angle up and right, then cut back left to a broad grassy bench. Traverse the bench onto the ridge and scramble along the crest to the foot of the first of
descent: The buttress leads onto the ridge crest. Scramble along the ridge to Outpost Peak's summit, then drop south to the Outpost-Memorial saddle, crossing the top of the glacier and avoiding crevasses. Scramble the east ridge of Memorial to its summit, descend steeply and scramble down its southwest ridge
name: North Buttress
overview: Long alpine ridge outing, not to be underestimated; rock is poor in places, with loose blocks. From Wates-Gibson hut go south to the moraine, up its prow, then onto a grassy bench and along to the ridge and first tower (1.5-2 hours). approach: From the Smith-Dorrien highway south of Canmore, park at the West Wind Pass trailhead and hike the good trail to the pass, where the east face of the Rimwall comes into view. Cross beneath the cliff on narrow, exposed animal trails, which are well worn at first and harder to follow near the end. A r
descent: From the top of the wall, a short hike with a few third-class moves leads to the summit of the Rimwall, and a good trail from there leads back to the parking area.
name: On the wings of Maybe
overview: Ten-pitch, 400 m alpine rock route on the east face of Rimwall near Canmore, mixing sport and trad, all belays bolted. approach: Park at the gravel pullout near the northern edge of Jasper National Park, on the Hinton side, and follow the short gravel road toward the peak. descent: Rappel from the Metolius rap hangers on the route, or scramble up to the summit and follow the scramble route down. Loose rock is common on this face, so a party rappelling will knock debris onto anyone below; do not climb under another group.
name: Chimney Route
overview: Takes the conspicuous ramp and chimney system that leans left on the NW Face, though it involves no true chimney climbing. P1: crack leaning left to the slab base, then up the slab's right side along the dihedral to a tatted, old pin; belay near it but do not trust the pin. Coming from the west, hike roughly a mile on the Cochise trail, then descend to the principal wash. The walk takes one hour for someone who knows it, maybe two otherwise.
descent: Rappel the route itself using two ropes.
name: Abracadaver
overview: Admired for relentless difficulty and awkward protection; it was first graded 5.9 before later ascents revised it. Pitches alternate between bolted opening moves, an offwidth, an airy layback to a roof, a difficult crack over the belay and the flank of a giant detached flake.

overview: Starts on the north face of the North Summit beneath a prominent off-width. The hardest climbing comes early, in the off-width and the squeeze chimney, and then it eases to the top.

name: Cap'm Pissgums
overview: Serious, long chimney and crack line on the north side of End Pinnacle: bolt-protected stemming in a shallow chimney, then chimneys and offwidths up to an overhanging crack crux and bulgy upper pitches.

overview: The line trails a deep, lonely crack that peters out well short of the summit. name: Finger Rock (Standard Route)
overview: A short summit pitch onto the slender top of Finger Rock, only about two feet across and wildly exposed. The long, brushy approach is the real undertaking.

name: Flakey Bats on Crack
overview: Takes the central fracture of the wall past grassy tufts to a tree ledge, then angles up left to a narrow ledge. The second pitch heads east along a ledge ramp, passes a hollow-sounding flake and reaches a tree on top.

descent: double-rope rappel westward from a 2-bolt anchor to the saddle, then walk down the gully
name: Moby Dick
overview: A varied, popular multi-pitch on Whale Dome that climbs a pair of left-leaning cracks toward the whale's mouth, then wanders up knobby faces and an overlap to the top.

descent: scramble class 2 gully to the summit, then the head's standard descent
name: Neck Route
overview: A two-pitch line from the saddle between the Head and the Hump, using a loose gully and then an exposed face with a water chute. Easy scrambling above reaches the summit of the Head.

name: Southeast Arete
overview: The most popular technical line on Baboquivari, prized for generally solid rock, good gear and fun moves up the peak's southeast edge.

descent: single-rope rappel from summit eyebolts
name: Varicose
overview: A graceful crack curving off to the right that gives its small rock its character; of the little formations strung along the eastern ridge, this one stands out. It is a short, handsome line.

descent: Cross the summit to the saddle linking the formation to the ridge, descend the slope and gully to the right, and circle back to the base
name: West Gully
overview: Long, wandering mountaineering route on the western flank of Elephant Head: low-angle slabs to a big gully, roughly eight roped pitches, with loose rock and runout slab moves. Harder moves usually mean you are off route.

approach: From the Fairy Meadow hut, go up the moraine to the Granite Glacier and then up the left side of the Turret Glacier until you can step onto the north ridge of Adamant. The climbing starts from there on the ridge crest.

Go up the left part of the Turret Glacier until Adamant's North Ridge can be reached, then follow its crest to the summit (Class 3 and 4 dominate, with some easy Class 5). approach: From the Fairy Meadow hut, follow the path toward Friendship Col and the Echo Glacier. Gog is the higher, closer-to-the-col summit of the Gog-Magog pair, and the route starts on its east face, reached by hiking across the snow below it and crossing the moat to the rock.
descent: Rappel back down the east face to the base. Cross the moat and walk down the snowfield toward the Friendship Col trail and the hut.
name: Gog East Face
overview: Work up and right over ledges and cracks on the east face to a V-chimney, then go through it to the summit. A 50 m rappel returns to the base.

approach: From Fairy Meadow, go up the moraine and onto the Granite Glacier toward the Horn-Unicorn col. descent: From the Horn summit, look for the large rocks and horns at the top of the face where the angle drops to class 3; they make good rappel anchors. name: Horn - SE Face and Unicorn

descent: Descent is by rappel. From the summit go down the west face to the belay ledge below the wide crack, then rappel the first pitch back down to the notch and the east side. Cross the moat and walk back down the snowfield toward the hut.
name: Magog
